did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with the heading “Of David,” after which David addresses his soul and “all that is within him”—that is, his entire inner being—and calls on himself to bless the Lord.
The phrase “and do not forget all his benefits” places remembrance at the center of serving God: blessing the Lord flows from recognizing the good things He provides.
The first two acts of kindness mentioned are forgiveness of sins and healing: “who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases.”
The verse describes the Lord as the one who redeems life “from the pit” and crowns it with steadfast love and mercy; redemption and kindness thus appear together.
The psalmist compares renewal to the way “your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.” This is a poetic image of renewal and abundance, not a literal description of physical change in a person.
The Lord is presented as the one who does what is right and upholds justice for all the oppressed, so the psalm connects His mercy with bringing justice to the downtrodden.
The verse distinguishes between Moses and the people of Israel: the Lord made His ways known to Moses, and His deeds—“His acts”—to the people of Israel.
The verse gathers several of the psalm’s central descriptions of God’s mercy: the Lord is “compassionate and gracious,” “slow to anger,” and “abounding in steadfast love.”

The Lord’s steadfast love is described by comparing it to the immense distance between heaven and earth: “As high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is His steadfast love toward those who fear Him.”

Human life is described as passing like “grass” and “a flower of the field,” but the verse later emphasizes that the Lord’s steadfast love and righteousness endure “from everlasting to everlasting” for those who fear Him and for their descendants.
